docs.text: LightnerX ¶ LightnerX is a modular static C++ library for building applications that communicate using the INER semantic protocol. The CMake project provides the LightnerX target; it neither produces nor requires its own executable. The library provides types for representing messages, interpreters, callbacks, connection management, and a transport layer based on GameNetworkingSockets. INER defines the meaning of messages exchanged between an Authority and an Obedient. It does not define sockets, connections, or an execution model. These capabilities are provided by LightnerX's networking components and can be connected to the application according to the developer's needs. Library, not a framework ¶ LightnerX provides reusable components. The consuming application decides: when to initialize and shut down components; how to run update() ; which threads to use; how to organize the connection lifecycle; which modules to use or replace with its own implementations. For example, you can pass bytes from your own transport to lightnerx::communication::MessageInterpreter . To interpret messages from the Obedient, obedientInterpret takes a lightnerx::network::ConnectionManager ; an application that manages connections on its own must maintain the mapping between handles and IDs used by the interpreter in that object. Key concepts ¶ Authority: controls internal states and receives intentions from the Obedient. Obedient: sends intentions to the Authority and receives events and responses. Event: an occurrence communicated by the Authority. Response: the result of an intention sent by the Obedient. Intention: an action request sent to the Authority. Notification: information sent to the Authority without requesting a state change. In LightnerX, the application connects components through callbacks: the network delivers bytes, and MessageInterpreter interprets those bytes according to the direction of communication. When sending, lightnerx::network::Target lets you select a connection, a group, or a broadcast with or without exceptions. Navigation ¶ Setup First steps Communication and the INER protocol API reference Server example ¶ This example receives notifications from the client and sends the text Hello, World! in events to registered connections. The snippets below make up the complete program at the end of the README; the statements belong inside the main function, after the imports shown in the complete code. Create the components ¶ The manager maps handles to internal client IDs. Register ID 47 so that the interpreter recognizes notifications sent by the client in this example. using namespace std::chrono_literals; namespace network = lightnerx::network; namespace communication = lightnerx::communication; network::Server server; network::ConnectionManager connections{30, 30}; communication::MessageInterpreter interpreter; communication::NotificationRegistry notifications; notifications.registerId(47); Track connections ¶ The callbacks keep the manager up to date. If registering a connection fails, the server requests its disconnection. server.addClientConnectedCallback([&](HSteamNetConnection connection) { if (!connections.add(connection)) { if (const auto result = server.disconnectConnection(connection, false); !result) { std::println("Failed to disconnect: {}", result.error().message()); } } }); server.addClientDisconnectedCallback([&](HSteamNetConnection connection) { if (const auto id = connections.getClientId(connection)) { connections.remove(*id); } }); Receive messages ¶ Forward the received bytes to obedientInterpret . The interpreter's callback delivers the message and the internal client ID. In this example, the payload is text and is read during the callback. server.addClientReceivedMessageCallback( [&](std::span<const std::byte> bytes, HSteamNetConnection connection) { interpreter.obedientInterpret(bytes, notifications, connection, connections); } ); interpreter.addObedientInterpretedMessageCallback( [](communication::Message message, std::uint16_t clientId) { const std::string_view text{ reinterpret_cast<const char*>(message.payload.data()), message.payload.size() }; std::println("Client {}: {}", clientId, text); } ); Start the server ¶ Start listening on port 41333 , with an established connection timeout of 3000 ms, and reserve one slot for the batcher's pending message. if (const auto result = server.start(41333, 3000); !result) { std::println("Failed to start: {}", result.error().message()); return 1; } network::initMessagesBatcher(1); Prepare an event ¶ Convert the text to bytes and include the header and payload in the total size. For Event , the size is shifted one bit to the left. Type 990 is chosen by the application. const std::string_view greeting = "Hello, World!"; const auto payload = std::as_bytes(std::span{greeting}); const communication::Event event{ // The least significant bit distinguishes Event from Response. static_cast<std::uint16_t>((sizeof(communication::Event) + payload.size()) << 1), 990 }; Update and send ¶ update() processes the network. The converter creates an OutboundMessage , which is passed directly to queueMessage . Target::broadcast() selects the connections registered at flush time. while (true) { if (const auto result = server.update(); !result) { std::println("Failed to update: {}", result.error().message()); break; } if (const auto result = network::queueMessage(communication::event2OutboundMessage( event, payload, network::Target::broadcast())); !result) { std::println("Failed to queue: {}", result.error().message()); break; } if (const auto result = network::flushAll(connections); !result) { std::println("Failed to send: {}", result.error().message()); break; } std::this_thread::sleep_for(3s); } queueMessage takes ownership of the message, including when it returns an error; the application does not call Release() afterward. flushAll processes the queue and releases the messages. The three-second interval is a choice made for this example; the application defines its own update rate. Shut down the server ¶ After exiting the loop due to an error, close the server. Returning 1 signals an exit due to failure in this example. server.close(); return 1; Client example ¶ The client connects to the server at 127.0.0.1:41333 , prints the received events, and sends a notification with the same text. Run the server and client in separate processes. Create the components ¶ The empty manager satisfies the flushAll signature. Sending to the server individually uses the client's connection handle directly. using namespace std::chrono_literals; namespace network = lightnerx::network; namespace communication = lightnerx::communication; network::Client client; network::ConnectionManager connections{0, 0}; // Required by flush, without broadcast. communication::MessageInterpreter interpreter; Receive messages from the server ¶ Forward the bytes to authorityInterpret , which interprets messages from the Authority. The callback below prints the text payload agreed upon by these examples and handles empty payloads. client.addServerReceivedMessageCallback([&](std::span<const std::byte> bytes) { interpreter.authorityInterpret(bytes); }); interpreter.addAuthorityInterpretedMessageCallback([](communication::Message message) { const auto text = message.payload.empty() ? std::string_view{} : std::string_view{ reinterpret_cast<const char*>(message.payload.data()), message.payload.size() }; std::println("Server: {}", text); }); The callbacks use the bytes during the call. To retain a received payload, copy its bytes into application storage before returning. Start and connect ¶ Initialize the client, request a connection to the server, and reserve space in the batcher. The connection will be tracked during calls to update() . if (const auto result = client.start(); !result) { std::println("Failed to start: {}", result.error().message()); return 1; } if (const auto result = client.connect("127.0.0.1", 41333); !result) { std::println("Failed to connect: {}", result.error().message()); return 1; } network::initMessagesBatcher(1); Prepare a notification ¶ Notification uses the total size directly, without bit shifting. ID 47 corresponds to the registration made on the server. const std::string_view greeting = "Hello, World!"; const auto payload = std::as_bytes(std::span{greeting}); const communication::Notification notification{ static_cast<std::uint16_t>(sizeof(communication::Notification) + payload.size()), 47 // The server must register this ID in NotificationRegistry. }; Update and send to the server ¶ Process up to 32 messages per update and send when isConnected() indicates an established connection. Target::single selects the server's handle. while (true) { if (const auto result = client.update(32); !result) { std::println("Failed to update: {}", result.error().message()); break; } if (client.isConnected()) { if (const auto result = network::queueMessage(communication::notification2OutboundMessage( notification, payload, network::Target::single(client.getServerHConn()))); !result) { std::println("Failed to queue: {}", result.error().message()); break; } if (const auto result = network::flushAll(connections); !result) { std::println("Failed to send: {}", result.error().message()); break; } } std::this_thread::sleep_for(3000ms); } Shut down the client ¶ When exiting due to an error, the Client destructor closes the connection and shuts down the network. Returning 1 indicates the failure that interrupted the example. return 1; // The Client destructor closes the connection and shuts down the network. docs.text: API reference ¶ This page presents the public components grouped by module. All modules are imported with import and belong to the indicated namespaces. Operations that return std::expected<void, std::error_code> can be checked with if (!result) . In the event of an error, result.error() provides the code and result.error().message() provides its description. Complete examples are available in First steps . lightnerx.communication.base_protocol ¶ lightnerx::communication::BaseProtocol ¶ Base structure for headers. BaseProtocol(std::uint16_t size); size : when constructing a message for sending, the encoded size of the Authority's message or the total size of the Obedient's message. The interpreter delivers this field with the size already decoded. Public field: std::uint16_t size . lightnerx.communication.mbt ¶ lightnerx::communication::MBT ¶ Stores the message's semantic identifier. MBT(std::uint16_t type); Public field: std::uint16_t type . Message types ¶ lightnerx.communication.event ¶ lightnerx::communication::Event ¶ Header for an event from the Authority. Event(std::uint16_t size, std::uint16_t typeId); Public fields: protocol : BaseProtocol ; mbt : MBT . lightnerx.communication.notification ¶ lightnerx::communication::Notification ¶ Header for a notification from the Obedient. Notification(std::uint16_t size, std::uint16_t type); Public fields: protocol : BaseProtocol ; mbt : MBT . lightnerx::communication::NotificationRegistry ¶ Registers IDs that the server should interpret as Notification . void registerId(std::uint16_t id); void registerIds(std::unordered_set<std::uint16_t>&& newIds); bool exist(std::uint16_t id) const noexcept; registerId adds an ID, and registerIds incorporates the IDs from a set passed as a temporary or with std::move . exist() reports whether the ID is registered. The application provides the registry to obedientInterpret . lightnerx.communication.intention ¶ lightnerx::communication::Intention ¶ Header for an intention sent to the Authority. Intention( std::uint16_t size, std::uint16_t type, std::uint16_t correlationId ); Public fields: protocol : BaseProtocol ; mbt : MBT ; correlationId : identifier used to correlate the response. lightnerx.communication.response ¶ lightnerx::communication::Response ¶ Header used for approved or failure responses. Response( std::uint16_t size, std::uint16_t correlationId, std::uint8_t status ); Public fields: protocol : BaseProtocol ; correlationId ; status . lightnerx::communication::UnsuccessfulResponse ¶ Header used for denied or partially approved responses. UnsuccessfulResponse( std::uint16_t size, std::uint16_t correlationId, std::uint8_t status, std::uint16_t reasonCode ); Public fields: protocol : BaseProtocol ; correlationId ; status ; reasonCode . Status constants ¶ constexpr std::uint8_t APPROVED_RESPONSE = 0; constexpr std::uint8_t DENIED_RESPONSE = 1; constexpr std::uint8_t PARTIALLY_APPROVED_RESPONSE = 2; constexpr std::uint8_t FAILURE_RESPONSE = 3; lightnerx.communication.message ¶ lightnerx::communication::Message ¶ Result delivered by the interpreter. struct Message { std::variant< Event, Intention, Response, UnsuccessfulResponse, Notification > header; std::span<const std::byte> payload; }; Use std::visit(visitor, message.header) to examine the type stored in header . The header is a value; payload references the buffer provided to the interpreter. docs.text: Communication and the INER protocol ¶ INER and LightnerX ¶ INER is a semantic protocol. It defines the meaning and organization of messages, but does not define sockets, addressing, threads, or the transmission mechanism. LightnerX implements the protocol's message types and provides networking components based on GameNetworkingSockets. The division is: Responsibility INER LightnerX Meaning of Event, Response, Intention, and Notification Yes Represented by C++ types Message identification Yes MBT::type , correlationId , and status fields Header encoding Yes Packed structures and converters Sockets and connections No Server , Client , and GameNetworkingSockets Execution model No Chosen by the application Roles ¶ Authority ¶ The Authority controls internal states. It receives Intention and Notification from the Obedient and sends Event and Response . In LightnerX, the server typically interprets received messages with: interpreter.obedientInterpret(bytes, registry, connection, connections); Obedient ¶ The Obedient sends intentions to the Authority and receives information about occurrences and results. In LightnerX, the client typically interprets received messages with: interpreter.authorityInterpret(bytes); Message types ¶ Event ¶ Event communicates an occurrence from the Authority. Its header contains: BaseProtocol::size ; MBT::type , used as type_id . The payload, when present, follows the header. Response ¶ Response relates the result to an intention through correlationId and contains a status . The statuses are exposed by constants in the lightnerx.communication.response module: Constant Value Meaning Type used by LightnerX APPROVED_RESPONSE 0 intention fully approved Response DENIED_RESPONSE 1 intention denied UnsuccessfulResponse PARTIALLY_APPROVED_RESPONSE 2 intention partially applied UnsuccessfulResponse FAILURE_RESPONSE 3 internal error during processing Response A failure does not necessarily mean that the intention was denied; the application may decide to try again. UnsuccessfulResponse adds reasonCode to the header of denied or partially approved responses. For partial approval, the meaning of the payload is defined by the application. Intention ¶ Intention requests that the Authority perform an action. Its header contains: BaseProtocol::size ; MBT::type ; correlationId . The intention's payload follows this header. Notification ¶ Notification communicates information to the Authority without requiring state validation, since it does not request a change to the Authority's internal states. Its header contains size and type , followed by the optional payload. On the server, NotificationRegistry specifies which type_id values should be interpreted as Notification : import std; import lightnerx.communication.notification; void registerNotifications(lightnerx::communication::NotificationRegistry& registry) { registry.registerId(47); registry.registerIds(std::unordered_set<std::uint16_t>{99, 100}); } The type_id values are defined by the application. There is no universal table of INER types. When receiving messages from the Obedient, registered IDs identify notifications; the others identify intentions. To send notifications, use notification2OutboundMessage . Binary representation ¶ Header structures are packed without additional padding using #pragma pack(push, 1) . The converters copy fields in the machine's native representation; participants must use a compatible representation for these fields and agree on the payload format. Messages from the Authority ¶ The first field uses a combined value: the least significant bit indicates whether the message is a Response , and the remaining fifteen bits represent the size. Message Header Content Event 2 bytes of combined size + 2 bytes of type variable payload Response 2 bytes of combined size + 2 bytes of correlationId + 1 byte of status no payload for the statuses represented by Response UnsuccessfulResponse Response structure + 2 bytes of reasonCode variable payload for a partial response When constructing the header, the combined value takes the form: Event: (total_size << 1) | 0 Response: (total_size << 1) | 1 The interpreter retrieves the size with base >> 1 and distinguishes Event from Response with base & 1 . In the headers delivered to the callback, protocol.size already contains the decoded size, without the type bit. Messages from the Obedient ¶ In messages from the Obedient, size directly represents the total message size. Message Header Content Notification 2 bytes of size + 2 bytes of type variable payload Intention 2 bytes of size + 2 bytes of type + 2 bytes of correlationId variable payload The specified size must include the header and payload. The converters copy the header and payload into a SteamNetworkingMessage_t ; they do not automatically construct the semantic value of the size field. Identifiers ¶ type_id identifies the semantic type defined by the application and appears in the code as MBT::type . correlationId relates a response to its corresponding intention. The ID received in the server's interpreted message callback is the internal identifier assigned by ConnectionManager . This internal ID belongs to the connection management implementation and is not an INER protocol field. The name originId does not designate a protocol field either. Callbacks run during the interpretation call. The header is delivered by value, but the span only references the received bytes. In the flow with Server or Client , these bytes are released after the receive callbacks. To retain the payload, copy its bytes during the callback; copying only Message keeps a reference to the same buffer. Sending flow ¶ The usual flow is: Initialize the network and call initMessagesBatcher(capacity) before queuing the first message. Construct the header with the total message size. Create a lightnerx::network::Target . Use the corresponding converter to obtain a lightnerx::network::OutboundMessage . Pass the object to queueMessage(std::move(outbound)) , transferring ownership of the message and destination. Check the queuing result and call flushAll(connectionManager) at the time chosen by the application. What each step does ¶ queueMessage receives the OutboundMessage from the converter and stores the same message with its destination, without allocating another message or copying the bytes. The call consumes the message: on success, the batcher keeps it until the flush; if the queue is full, it releases it immediately. The caller must not call Release() or reuse the message after passing it to the queue. A null pointer is rejected with invalid_argument . flushAll iterates over pending messages, routes each one according to its destination, and releases the message received from the converter with Release() . All entries are processed and the queue is emptied even when send errors occur. The return value indicates success or the last error encountered among these operations. Batching lets you accumulate multiple messages before a flush. Each entry remains a separate message; payloads are not concatenated. The application decides when to flush, for example at the end of an update. Success indicates that the transport accepted the send operations, without confirming processing by the recipient. docs.text: INER is a semantic protocol. It defines the meaning and organization of messages, but does not define sockets, addressing, threads, or the transmission mechanism. LightnerX implements the protocol's message types and provides networking components based on GameNetworkingSockets. docs.text: Response relates the result to an intention through correlationId and contains a status . docs.text: Header structures are packed without additional padding using #pragma pack(push, 1) . The converters copy fields in the machine's native representation; participants must use a compatible representation for these fields and agree on the payload format.

docs.text: The first field uses a combined value: the least significant bit indicates whether the message is a Response , and the remaining fifteen bits represent the size. Message Header Content Event 2 bytes of combined size + 2 bytes of type variable payload Response 2 bytes of combined size + 2 bytes of correlationId + 1 byte of status no payload for the statuses represented by Response UnsuccessfulResponse Response structure + 2 bytes of reasonCode variable payload for a partial response When constructing the header, the combined value takes the form: Event: (total_size << 1) | 0 Response: (total_size << 1) | 1 The interpreter retrieves the size with base >> 1 and distinguishes Event from Response with base & 1 . In the headers delivered to the callback, protocol.size already contains the decoded size, without the type bit.

docs.text: First steps ¶ This guide shows the essential flow for setting up a server and a client. The examples use LightnerX components directly and leave the execution model to the application. The two programs illustrate separate consuming applications; the library remains a static library. Server ¶ The server receives bytes from clients, forwards those bytes to MessageInterpreter , and receives interpreted messages through a callback. #include "steam/steamnetworkingtypes.h" import std; import lightnerx.communication.intention; import lightnerx.communication.message; import lightnerx.communication.notification; import lightnerx.network.connection_manager; import lightnerx.network.server; int main() { lightnerx::network::Server server; lightnerx::network::ConnectionManager connections{10, 10}; lightnerx::communication::MessageInterpreter interpreter; lightnerx::communication::NotificationRegistry registry; registry.registerId(47); server.addClientConnectedCallback( [&connections, &server](HSteamNetConnection connection) { if (!connections.add(connection)) { const auto disconnected = server.disconnectConnection(connection, false); if (!disconnected) { std::println("Failed to disconnect: {}", disconnected.error().message()); } } } ); server.addClientDisconnectedCallback( [&connections](HSteamNetConnection connection) { if (const auto id = connections.getClientId(connection)) { connections.remove(*id); } } ); server.addClientReceivedMessageCallback( [&interpreter, &registry, &connections]( std::span<const std::byte> bytes, HSteamNetConnection connection ) { interpreter.obedientInterpret( bytes, registry, connection, connections ); } ); interpreter.addObedientInterpretedMessageCallback( [](lightnerx::communication::Message message, std::uint16_t clientId) { std::println("Message received from client {}", clientId); std::visit([](const auto& header) { using Header = std::remove_cvref_t<decltype(header)>; if constexpr (std::is_same_v<Header, lightnerx::communication::Intention>) { std::println("Intention {}, correlation {}", header.mbt.type, header.correlationId); } else if constexpr (std::is_same_v<Header, lightnerx::communication::Notification>) { std::println("Notification {}", header.mbt.type); } }, message.header); } ); const auto started = server.start(45333, 2500); if (!started) { std::println("Failed to start: {}", started.error().message()); return 1; } while (true) { if (const auto updated = server.update(); !updated) { std::println("Update failed: {}", updated.error().message()); break; } } server.close(); } The connection callback must update the ConnectionManager , because the interpreter uses this object to map the connection to the ID delivered to the interpreted message callback. The lambdas capture the components by reference to connect them. Keep these objects alive as long as their callbacks may run. The received payload points to the network message's bytes; copy the bytes during the callback if you need to use them later. Client ¶ The client forwards bytes received from the server to the authorityInterpret method. #include "steam/steamnetworkingtypes.h" import std; import lightnerx.communication.event; import lightnerx.communication.message; import lightnerx.communication.response; import lightnerx.network.client; int main() { lightnerx::network::Client client; lightnerx::communication::MessageInterpreter interpreter; client.addServerReceivedMessageCallback( [&interpreter](std::span<const std::byte> bytes) { interpreter.authorityInterpret(bytes); } ); interpreter.addAuthorityInterpretedMessageCallback( [](lightnerx::communication::Message message) { std::visit([](const auto& header) { using Header = std::remove_cvref_t<decltype(header)>; if constexpr (std::is_same_v<Header, lightnerx::communication::Event>) { std::println("Event {}", header.mbt.type); } else if constexpr ( std::is_same_v<Header, lightnerx::communication::Response> || std::is_same_v<Header, lightnerx::communication::UnsuccessfulResponse> ) { std::println("Response to intention {}: status {}", header.correlationId, header.status); if constexpr (std::is_same_v<Header, lightnerx::communication::UnsuccessfulResponse>) { std::println("Reason {}", header.reasonCode); } } }, message.header); } ); if (const auto started = client.start(); !started) { std::println("Failed to start: {}", started.error().message()); return 1; } if (const auto connected = client.connect("127.0.0.1", 45333); !connected) { std::println("Failed to connect: {}", connected.error().message()); return 1; } while (true) { if (const auto updated = client.update(1); !updated) { std::println("Update failed: {}", updated.error().message()); break; } } } connect() initiates the connection, and update() processes network callbacks and available messages. isConnected() can be used to query the state observed by the client. Execution model ¶ The server.update() and client.update() methods are called by the application. They can run on the main thread, on a dedicated thread, or within the consuming project's existing execution loop. The library does not require a specific number of threads or a fixed interval between updates. Receive callbacks run during update() , and interpretation callbacks run on the thread that calls the interpreter. When sharing components across threads, handle synchronization in the application. For the batcher, serialize initialization, queuing, and flush calls, which operate on the same queue. Batch sending ¶ With the network initialized by Server::start() , Client::start() , or lightnerx::network::networkInit() , reserve space in the batcher before queuing the first message. Import lightnerx.network.message_batch and call: lightnerx::network::initMessagesBatcher(64); The destination is defined by lightnerx::network::Target . The following function creates an Event , routes it to a group, and sends the queue. It assumes the initialization above and returns the result of queuing or flushing to the caller. The same flow applies to the other message converters. #include "steam/steamnetworkingtypes.h" import std; import lightnerx.communication.event; import lightnerx.communication.message; import lightnerx.network.connection_manager; import lightnerx.network.message_batch; import lightnerx.network.target; std::expected<void, std::error_code> sendEventToGroup( std::span<const std::byte> payload, std::vector<HSteamNetConnection> receivers, const lightnerx::network::ConnectionManager& connections ) { const auto totalSize = sizeof(lightnerx::communication::Event) + payload.size(); if (totalSize > 0x7fff) { return std::unexpected(std::make_error_code(std::errc::message_size)); } const lightnerx::communication::Event event{ static_cast<std::uint16_t>(totalSize << 1), 47 }; auto outbound = lightnerx::communication::event2OutboundMessage( event, payload, lightnerx::network::Target::group(std::move(receivers)) ); const auto queued = lightnerx::network::queueMessage(std::move(outbound)); if (!queued) { return queued; } return lightnerx::network::flushAll(connections); } queueMessage receives the OutboundMessage created by the converter and takes ownership of the message and its destination, without reallocating the message or copying its bytes. If the queue is full, the call releases the message immediately and returns an error. If queuing is accepted, flushAll releases the message after the send attempt. Pass an existing object with std::move(outbound) or pass the converter's result directly to queueMessage . After the call, do not access, release, or requeue the consumed message, including in the event of an error. Since message is a raw pointer, std::move does not automatically set it to null in the original object. The header and payload provided to the converter remain owned by the application. With handles obtained by the client or through the server's connection callbacks, the available destinations are: auto oneClient = lightnerx::network::Target::single(connection); auto selectedClients = lightnerx::network::Target::group({firstConnection, secondConnection}); auto everyone = lightnerx::network::Target::broadcast(); auto everyoneElse = lightnerx::network::Target::broadcast({connectionToSkip}); These calls only describe destinations. You can queue several messages and run flushAll(connections) at the end of an application step; the immediate flush shown in the function is a choice made for the example. Next steps ¶ See Communication and the INER protocol to understand headers, destinations, and sending flows. See API reference for networking components, messages, Target , and the batcher.
